title.en: The Death of Cuchulainn: the Hound at Bay

region.en: Murthemne Plain near Dun Delgan (Dundalk), Co. Louth, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭勞斯郡敦·德爾岡（鄧多克）附近穆爾西姆尼平原

texts.period: Aided Con Culainn traditions, medieval Irish MSS; Eleanor Hull retelling 1910

source.work: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster (1910), Chapters XXVIII-XXIX, eBook #52963

summary.en: Three venomous spears from the otherworld — 'Wind', 'Good-luck' and 'Cast' — must each kill a king; friends hide the dying hero in the Glen of the Deaf until the Children of the Blast conjure him a phantom sea, and he goes out to die: three spears kill horse, charioteer and king of heroes in turn, and Cuchulainn binds himself standing to a pillar-stone to die upright before his enemies.
summary.zh: 彼岸三毒矛——『風』、『好運』、『擲』——各須殺一王；摯友將垂死英雄藏於失聰谷，直至「疾風之子」幻化海象誘其出戰；三矛依次殺馬、御者、英雄之王，庫丘林立身縛於石柱，直立而死於敵前。

sensitivity.note: The death by three geasa spears is a classic Irish doom-weapon narrative; the standing death is the icon of the cycle, carved on the Standing Stone of the Hero's Sigh.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910: Medb sent a brood of monstrous sprites, half-women, half-goblins, one-eyed in their foreheads, right legs and left arms lopped at the stump, to learn throughout the world the arts that bring men to death; five years they wandered and reached the realm where Vulcan forged his weapons, and from his hand took three spears named Wind, Good-luck and Cast, and three swords, the Wounder, the Hacker and the Hewer. 'By these three spears the splendid Hound shall die; each one of them shall kill a king of Erin, and among those kings the mighty king of Erin's hero-chiefs, whom men call Ulster's Hound.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, chs. XXVIII-XXIX; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Emer and his friends hid the hero in the Glen of the Deaf with music and chess, his weapons taken away. A raven croaked war into his ear; a phantom army of puff-balls and thistle-stalks was raised round the house; on the last day a magic sea rose wave on wave to the door, and Cuchulainn rose with madness upon him — 'I see the horses of Manannan riding on the waves; I hear Manannan's fairy harp; Manannan's ancient face I see beckoning me over the main' — and Emer knew the hour of his fate was come, and armed him herself. The horses wept tears of dusky blood and dropped his weapons at his feet; a maiden of the war-goddess washed his own garments crimson in the stream; he went on, the hero's light brighter than the sun on his forehead. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XXIX; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Through the day he was alone against a host, and no sword would pierce his skin; then the Wild Women gave the three spears: Curoi's spear pinned the Grey of Macha to the ground; Erc's second spear wounded Cuchulainn and killed Laeg, and he sent his charioteer home with his blessing; Luga's third spear pierced Cuchulainn to the earth. The host stood in a silent ring while he drank at the loch and washed; then he leaned his back against a tall pillar-stone beside the water, bound himself to it with the girdle about his breast, sword in hand — 'I will not die before the men of Erin lying down nor sitting on the ground, but I will die before them standing up.' The Grey of Macha came and laid its head on his breast, weeping; the carrion birds gathered, but the host dared not come near for the hero's light that shone from his forehead; Luga came near, the great sword fell from the dying hand and struck his hand off — and with one deep sigh Cuchulainn's soul parted, and the pillar-stone split, as may be seen to this day. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Hull 1910, ch. XXIX; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Eleanor Hull, Cuchulain, the Hound of Ulster, London 1910 (public domain); underlying: Aided Con Culainn (Book of Leinster version, ed. and trans. Whitley Stokes, 1902, public domain)

narrative.en:
The death-tale of the Hound of Ulster is built like a judicial execution that the whole otherworld has signed — and the hero, knowing every clause, walks into it upright.

The doom begins in an inventory. Medb, nursing her humiliation at the ford, stirred every enemy Cuchulainn had made and sent a brood of monstrous sprites — half-women, half-goblins, one-eyed in their foreheads, one leg and one arm lopped at the stump — to travel the world for five years and learn all the magic arts that bring men to death. In the realm of Vulcan they took three spears named Wind, Good-luck and Cast, and three swords, the Wounder, the Hacker and the Hewer; and the word of the forge was law: 'By these three spears the splendid Hound shall die; each one of them shall kill a king of Erin, and among those kings the mighty king of Erin's hero-chiefs, the triumphant, heavy-smiting noble youth, whom men call Ulster's Hound.'

The first weapon was concealment. Emer and his friends carried the exhausted hero — still sick from his wounds and his fairy sickness — to the Glen of the Deaf, where no sound of war could reach, took his chariot and weapons away, and set the women to music and chess to hold him. The Children of the Blast worked their lures in order: a raven croaking that Dun Dalgan burned; an army of puff-balls and thistle-stalks shouting round the house; and on the last day a phantom sea, wave on wave rolling to the door — 'I see the horses of Manannan riding on the waves; I hear Manannan's fairy harp play gently over the billows; Manannan's ancient face I see beckoning me over the main.' The seer's word had been: when he saw the horses of the ancient Ocean god, his hour was come. Emer herself armed him then, that he might die a chariot-chief and not a deceived man.

The omens fell in order: the horses wept tears of dusky blood and dropped his weapons at his feet; on the road a maiden of the war-goddess wrung his own garments crimson in a red-running stream — Laeg turned to flee, and the hero said, 'whether I stay I am devoted to death, or whether I go, the span of my life is run out... let me but once more avenge my country's wrongs, and gladly, with joy, I give my life.'

Then the battle, and the law of the three spears. Alone against a host from dewy morn to fall of night, no sword piercing his skin, twice he had the victory and was dragged back; the third time the Wild Women placed the spears in the hands of Curoi's son Luga, of young Erc king of Tara, and of dark Curoi. Curoi's spear missed Cuchulainn and pinned the Grey of Macha to the earth — the horse's death counted as a king's. Erc's spear wounded Cuchulainn's hip and went through to kill Laeg, who took his master's blessing and rode home to Emer to say her husband loved her yet. Luga's spear, thrown at last, rose over all the heads of the host and pierced Cuchulainn to the earth; and the whole army fell silent, standing in a ring, none daring to touch him.

He asked leave to drink at the loch — 'if I come not to you again, I bid you come for me' — drank, washed, and cast himself against a tall pillar-stone beside the water, bound his breast to it with his girdle, took sword in one hand and shield at the other, and said: 'I will not die before the men of Erin lying down nor sitting on the ground, but I will die before them standing up.' The Grey of Macha dragged its spear to him and laid its head, weeping bloody tears, on his breast; carrion birds gathered; the host stood off in awe of the hero's light. When Luga crept near to see whether he lived, the dying hand dropped the sword and struck Luga's hand off — a dead man's last blow — and with a deep sigh Cuchulainn's soul parted from his body, and the sigh split the pillar-stone, as may be seen to this day: the Pillar of the Hero's Dying Sigh.
narrative.zh: 阿爾斯特獵犬之死的故事，其構造如一場全彼岸簽署之處決——而英雄知曉每一條款，仍直立赴死。厄運始於一份清單。梅芙懷渡口受辱之恨，煽動庫丘林所有仇敵，並遣一隊半女半妖、額中獨目之妖物，環遊世界五年、學盡致人於死之魔法。在火神鍛造之地，她們取得三矛：名為『風』、『好運』、『擲』；爐邊之話即法：『此三矛將殺壯麗之獵犬；每矛各殺愛爾蘭一王，而諸王之中，將是人稱阿爾斯特獵犬者。』第一件武器是隱匿。艾默與眾友將力竭之英雄送往失聰谷——該谷不聞戰聲——收走其戰車兵器，令女子以音樂棋局留他。疾風之子依次施誘：烏鴉嘶叫敦·德爾岡已焚；絨球與薊莖組成幻軍繞屋吶喊；末日之時幻海生波、浪浪逼門——『我見瑪南南之馬騎於浪上；我聞瑪南南之仙琴於波間輕奏；我見瑪南南古老之面於海上向我招手。』先知之言曾是：見太古海神之馬之日，即其時辰至之日。艾默遂親自為其披甲，使其以戰車首領而非受欺者之身而死。凶兆依次落下：雙馬泣血淚、兵器落於其足；途中戰神之侍女於紅流之溪中絞洗他自己的衣裳——萊格欲逃，英雄曰：『留亦死，去亦死……讓我再一次復國之仇，欣喜奉上吾命。』繼而戰鬥與三矛之法。自露晨至夜幕孤身敵一軍；第三次，疾風之女將三矛分予庫洛伊之子盧加、塔拉幼王埃爾克、與黑暗之庫洛伊。庫洛伊之矛落空而釘灰駒灰之瑪哈於地——馬之死算作一王。埃爾克之矛傷庫丘林之髖、貫而殺萊格；萊格領主人之祝福騎歸艾默處。盧加之矛越全軍之頂、將庫丘林釘於大地；全軍肅立成環、無人敢近。他求往湖邊解渴——『若我不復返，請你們來找我』——飲水洗身，而後倚水邊高聳之石柱、以胸帶縛身於柱、一手持劍一手持盾：『我不願於阿爾斯特人前臥死或坐死，我願立於他們面前而死。』灰之瑪哈拖矛而來、以泣血之頭伏於其胸；食腐之鳥群集；全軍畏英雄之光而卻步。盧加潛近視其生死，垂死之手鬆劍、斬落盧加一手——死者最後一擊——隨一聲長嘆，庫丘林之魂離其身，嘆聲裂石柱，至今可見：英雄臨終之嘆之柱。

functions: Doom-weapon theology: the three named spears as geasa that must kill kings — fate administered as law
Icon of the standing death: sovereignty retained through the posture of dying, splitting the pillar-stone
The hero's light (loechra) as battle-aura: the visible sign that keeps armies at bay
Etiology of the standing stone at the loch in Murthemne and of the horse's loyalty at death

title.en: The Death of Conor mac Nessa: the Brain-Ball Bursts
title.zh: 科恩·麥克·內薩之死：腦丸爆裂

region.en: Athnurchar (the Ford of the Sling-cast), Co. Westmeath, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭西米斯郡阿斯努查（彈射渡口）

texts.period: Aided Conchobuir tradition, medieval Irish MSS; Rolleston retelling 1911

source.work: T. W. Rolleston, Myths & Legends of the Celtic Race (1911), Chapter VI, eBook #34081

summary.en: Conall of the Victories kills the king of Leinster unjustly and mixes the dead king's brains with lime into a sling-stone; the Connacht champion Ket finds it in Emain's treasury and years later slings it into Conor's forehead; the ball is sewn up with golden thread under a taboo of passion and horse-riding — until the king hears of a hill far away where a man hangs between two criminals, and the brain-ball bursts with his fury.
summary.zh: 勝利者科納爾不義地殺死萊因斯特王，取其腦髓混石灰製彈石；康諾特勇士康特於埃馬因寶庫尋得之，數年後彈射入科恩前額；腦丸以金線縫合、王受戒不得激憤騎馬——直至他聞知遠方山丘上有男子懸於二罪犯之間，激憤之下腦丸爆裂。

sensitivity.note: The Christianizing ending (Conor's death at the news of the Crucifixion) is a famous interpolation that welds the pagan Ulster cycle onto Christian chronology; retold from public-domain print.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911: An unjust and cruel attack had been made by Conor on Mesgedra, king of Leinster, in which that monarch met his death at the hand of Conall of the Victories. Conall took out the brains of the dead king and mingled them with lime to make a sling-stone — such 'brain balls' being accounted the most deadly of missiles — and the ball was laid up in the king's treasure-house at Emain Macha, where the Connacht champion Ket son of Maga found it one day when prowling in disguise through Ulster, and kept it always by him. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: The Connacht men took a spoil of cattle from Ulster, and the Ulstermen under Conor overtook them at a river-ford still called Athnurchar, the Ford of the Sling-cast, in Westmeath. Many of the ladies of Connacht came to their side of the river to view the famous Ulster warriors, and Conor drew near to show himself; Ket, lurking in ambush, rose and slung the brain-ball at Conor, striking him full in the forehead. His physician Fingen pronounced that if the ball were extracted he must die; it was sewn up with golden thread, and the king was bidden to keep himself from horse-riding and from all vehement passion and exertion, and he would do well. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rolleston 1911; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Seven years afterwards Conor saw the sun darken at noonday and summoned his druid, who in a magic trance saw a hill in a distant land with three crosses on it, and a human form nailed to each, and one of them like the Immortals. 'Is he a malefactor?' asked Conor. 'Nay, but the Son of the living God,' said the druid, and told the king the story of the death of Christ. Conor broke out in fury, and drawing his sword hacked at the oak-trees in the sacred grove crying 'Thus would I deal with his enemies!' — and with the excitement and exertion the brain-ball burst from his head, and he fell dead. And thus was the vengeance of Mesgedra fulfilled. With Conor and with Cuchulainn the glory of the Red Branch and the dominance of Ulster passed away. Not verbatim.

narrative.en:
The death of Conor mac Nessa is the Ulster cycle's most curious ending: a pagan king killed by an unhealed wound reopened at the news of a foreign execution — myth stitching itself onto history.

The wound begins as an atrocity. An unjust and cruel attack was made by Conor on Mesgedra, king of Leinster, in which that monarch met his death at the hand of Conall of the Victories. Conall took out the brains of the dead king and mingled them with lime to make a sling-stone — such 'brain balls' being accounted the most deadly of missiles in Irish warfare — and the ball was laid up in the king's treasure-house at Emain Macha. There the Connacht champion Ket son of Maga, prowling through Ulster in disguise, found it one day and kept it always by him: a king's death carried as a pocket weapon.

Its hour came at a cattle-spoil. The Connacht men drove a spoil from Ulster, and the Ulstermen under Conor overtook them at a river-ford in Westmeath still called Athnurchar, the Ford of the Sling-cast. The ladies of Connacht crowded to their bank to see the famous Ulster warriors, and Conor — the stateliest man of his time — drew near the water to show himself to the women; and Ket, lurking in ambush, rose and slung the brain-ball into the king's forehead. Conor fell and was carried living to Emain, where his physician Fingen pronounced that if the ball were extracted he must die; it was sewn up with golden thread, and the king was bidden to keep himself from horse-riding and from all vehement passion and exertion — a geis on emotion itself, and one of the strangest medical prescriptions in medieval literature.

Seven years he lived so. Then, one noon, Conor saw the sun darken, and summoned his druid, who in a magic trance traveled in vision to a hill in a distant land on which stand three crosses, with a human form nailed to each, and one of them like the Immortals. 'Is he a malefactor?' asked Conor. 'Nay,' says the druid, 'but the Son of the living God,' and he told the king the story of the death of Christ. Conor broke out in fury — the only recorded act of the King of Ulster's wrath being incurred on behalf of a foreign god — and drawing his sword hacked at the oak-trees in the sacred grove, crying, 'Thus would I deal with his enemies!' And with the excitement and exertion the brain-ball burst from his head, and he fell dead. Thus was the vengeance of Mesgedra fulfilled: the murdered king of Leinster reached through seven years and one darkened noon to kill his killer's killer's king. With Conor and with Cuchulainn the glory of the Red Branch and the dominance of Ulster passed away, and the next cycle — the Ossianic — brought different characters, different forests, and different ideals of life.
narrative.zh: 科恩·麥克·內薩之死乃阿爾斯特故事圈最奇特之結局：異國處決的消息使一處未癒之傷復裂，殺死異教之王——神話自行縫入歷史。創傷始於暴行。科恩不義地攻擊萊因斯特王梅斯蓋德拉，該王死於勝利者科納爾之手。科納爾取出死者腦髓、混以石灰製成彈石——此類『腦丸』被視為愛爾蘭戰爭中最致命之投射武器——而彈石被藏於埃馬因·瑪哈王之寶庫。康諾特勇士康特·馬加之子偽裝潛行阿爾斯特時一日尋得之，隨身攜帶：以一位國王之死為口袋兵器。其時機於一場牛群劫掠中到來。康諾特人自阿爾斯特驅走牛群，科恩率阿爾斯特人於西米斯郡至今仍稱阿斯努查（彈射渡口）之河渡追上。康諾特貴婦擁至河岸觀看阿爾斯特名將，科恩近水展示己身；埋伏之康特起身、以腦丸彈射入王之前額。科恩倒地、活著被抬回埃馬因，醫師芬根判定：若取出彈丸必死；彈丸以金線縫合，王受戒：不得騎馬、不得有任何激烈情緒與勞累——對情緒本身之geis。如此七年。一日正午，科恩見日頭變暗，召其德魯伊；德魯伊於魔法出神中神遊至遠方一山丘，丘上有三具十字架、各釘一人形，其一似不朽者。『他是罪犯嗎？』科恩問。『非也，』德魯伊答，『乃永生上帝之子。』並向王講述基督之死。科恩勃然大怒——阿爾斯特之王之憤怒惟一一次為異國之神而發——拔劍砍伐聖林橡樹，呼曰：『我將如此對待他的敵人！』激憤與勞累之間，腦丸自其頭顱迸出，王倒地而死。梅斯蓋德拉之復仇就此完成。科恩與庫丘林既亡，紅枝之榮光與阿爾斯特之霸權隨之而去；下一個故事圈——奧西恩系——帶來不同人物、不同森林與不同的生活理想。

functions: Theology of the unhealed wound: vengeance delayed through an object (the brain-ball) rather than a person
Christian chronology hinge: the pagan king dies at the news of the Crucifixion, dating the heroic age to the life of Christ
Geis on passion: a kingship of regulated emotion — the medical taboo as constitutional restraint
Etiology of Athnurchar (the Ford of the Sling-cast) in Westmeath

title.en: Bricriu of the Poison-Tongue: Incitement and Death Under the Bulls
title.zh: 毒舌布里克魯：挑撥與公牛之下的死亡

region.en: Tarbga in Mag Ai (Rathcroghan), Connacht, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭康諾特馬格艾之塔爾布加（拉思克羅根）

texts.period: Tain Bo Cuailnge Recension I (Book of the Dun Cow, c. 1100); Faraday translation 1904

source.work: Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (1904), eBook #14391

summary.en: Bricriu Poison-tongue, the Ulster cycle's professional inciter, heckles Cuchulainn into breaking the Morrígan's shapes in the ford — then, years later, after Fergus has broken his head at chess, he crawls west in sadness to watch the two god-bulls fight at Tarbga, and the bulls go fighting over him and he dies; that is the Death of Bricriu.
summary.zh: 阿爾斯特故事圈之職業挑撥者——毒舌布里克魯——於渡口以譏言激庫丘林擊破摩里岡之百形；多年後，弗格斯弈棋擊破其頭，他悲傷西行觀二神牛於塔爾布加相鬥，二牛竟越其身而鬥，遂死——是為布里克魯之死。

sensitivity.note: Bricriu's death beneath the fighting bulls closes both the trickster and the bull-war theodicy of the Táin; the incitement scene includes the eel/wolf/heifer shapes owed to Táin Bó Regamna.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904: Bricriu Poison-tongue Mac Carbatha rose and began inciting Cuchulainn: 'Your strength is gone, when it is a little salmon that overthrows you when the Ulstermen are at hand coming to you out of their sickness yonder. Grievous for you to undertake a hero's deed in the presence of the men of Ireland and to ward off a formidable warrior in arms thus!' Therewith Cuchulainn arose and struck the eel so that its ribs broke in it, and the cattle were driven over the hosts eastwards; the she-wolf attacked him, and he threw a stone from his sling so that her eye broke in her head; and she came in the form of a hornless red heifer before the cows upon the pools and fords, and he threw a stone at the hornless red heifer so that her leg broke under her. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: Then Cuchulainn did to the Morrígan the three things that he had promised her in the Táin Bó Regamna, and fought Loch in the ford with the gae bolga. At the end of the Táin the Bull of Cooley met the White-horned at Tarbga in Mag Ai, and every one who escaped the fight was intent on nothing but beholding the two bulls fighting. Bricriu Poison-tongue was in the west in his sadness after Fergus had broken his head with his draughtmen; he came with the rest to see the combat of the bulls. The two bulls went in fighting over Bricriu, so that he died therefrom. That is the Death of Bricriu. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge, London 1904 (public domain); underlying: Táin Bó Cúailnge Recension I (Leabhar na hUidre, RIA MS 23 E 25, c. 1100)

narrative.en:
Bricriu of the Poison-tongue is the Ulster cycle's engine of plot — the satirist whose profession is to make heroes do stupid things — and the Táin grants him the strangest death in the cycle: crushed by the gods' own bulls.

His trade is incitement. In the middle of the Táin, when Cuchulainn is struggling at the ford with the Morrígan's shapes, Fergus can only tell his men to taunt the hero so that 'he may not fall for nothing' — and Bricriu rises to the work with relish: 'Your strength is gone, when it is a little salmon that overthrows you when the Ulstermen are at hand coming to you out of their sickness yonder. Grievous for you to undertake a hero's deed in the presence of the men of Ireland and to ward off a formidable warrior in arms thus!' Stung, Cuchulainn rises and does to the Morrígan the three things he had promised her in the Táin Bó Regamna: he strikes the eel so that its ribs break in it; when she comes as a she-wolf he breaks her eye with a sling-stone; when she comes as a hornless red heifer walking before the cows through the fords, he breaks her leg. The goddess retreats — three shapes, three wounds, the debt of the earlier tale paid — and the god-loans of the hero's anger are banked at Bricriu's word.

The great comic ending waits for the end of the war. After the Táin's battle, the two bulls of the gods met at Tarbga in Mag Ai, and every man who had escaped the war stood about only to watch them fight. Bricriu, in his sadness in the west — after Fergus had broken his head with the draughtmen at a game of chess, an insult recorded in the Echtra Nerai — came with the rest to see the combat. And the two bulls went in fighting over Bricriu, so that he died therefrom: the professional auditor of other men's duels is audited by the duel itself. 'That is the Death of Bricriu,' says the Táin, with the dry economy of a law-report — the only death in the cycle administered by cattle, and the exact penalty of a life spent whetting other men's violence.
narrative.zh: 毒舌布里克魯乃阿爾斯特故事圈之情節引擎——其職業即誘使英雄做蠢事之諷刺家——《奪牛記》賜他全圈最奇之死：被神之公牛碾斃。其業為挑撥。《奪牛記》中段，庫丘林在渡口與摩里岡之形搏鬥，弗格斯只能命部下嘲諷英雄『使其不至徒勞而死』——布里克魯欣然起身應工：『你的力量完了！區區一條鮭魚竟能擊倒你——阿爾斯特的人正從病中向你走來！在愛爾蘭眾人面前行英雄之舉、持械迎擊強敵——何等可悲！』庫丘林被刺而起身，行他在雷甘那牛劫記中許諾摩里岡的三事：擊鰻至肋骨斷於其中；她化母狼襲來，他以彈石碎其目；她化無角赤牝牛、牛群之前行於渡池，他擲石斷其腿。女神退卻——三形三傷，前篇之債已償——英雄之怒的信用記於布里克魯的話上。偉大的滑稽結局等著戰爭之末。戰後，二神牛於馬格艾之塔爾布加相會，凡自戰火逃脫之人皆只為觀牛鬥而立。布里克魯西行而悲——因弗格斯弈棋時以棋子擊破其頭，此辱記於奈拉的歷險——隨眾而來觀鬥。二牛竟於布里克魯之上相鬥而行，他因此而死。『是為布里克魯之死，』《奪牛記》以法律報告之乾燥筆法記之——全圈唯一由牛執行的死刑，亦是一生磨利他人暴力者之精確刑罰。

functions: Charter of the satirist's power: one insult redirects a hero's wrath against the divine
Comic theodicy of the Táin: the bull-duel as instrument of justice on the professional inciter
Interlace mechanism: Bricriu's taunt fuses two pre-tales (Regamna and the ford combats) into one action
Etiology of Tarbga (Bull-sorrow/Bull-fight) in Mag Ai

title.en: The Apparition of the Great Queen: the Driving of the Morrígan's Cow
title.zh: 偉大女王之顯形：驅趕摩里岡之牛

region.en: Dun Imrid (near Dundalk), Co. Louth, Ireland
region.zh: 愛爾蘭勞斯郡敦·伊姆里德（鄧多克附近）

texts.period: Táin Bó Regamna, Yellow Book of Lecan (14th c.) and Egerton 1782; Leahy translation 1905

source.work: A. H. Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland, Volume II (1905), 'The Apparition of the Great Queen to Cuchulain', eBook #5679

summary.en: A cry from the north wakes Cuchulainn at Dun Imrid; a one-legged chestnut horse hauls a chariot with the pole passed through its body, a red woman drives a cow before her, and her name is unpronounceable; when he spears her she names herself the Morrígan, guardian of his death, and prophesies the Raid of Cúailnge — and the three shapes she will take against him: eel, wolf, white red-eared heifer.
summary.zh: 北方呼聲驚醒敦·伊姆里德的庫丘林；一條獨腿栗色馬拉車、轅貫其身，紅衣女子驅牛於前，名不可讀；他以矛相脅，她自名摩里岡、其死之守護者，預言庫利牛劫——並預言她將化之三形：鰻、狼、白身紅耳牝牛。

sensitivity.note: The Morrígan offers Cuchulainn her love in the fuller tradition ('I will come to you and take the semblance of a woman'); her shape-shifts here are exactly those paid back in the Táin's ford combats.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905: At Dun Imrid lay Cuchulainn and slept, when a cry rang out from the north; he fell as he woke from his slumber with the thud of a weight to the ground, and sought the chariot. At the ford of the Double Wonder a chariot rattled toward them from the clay-soiled Coolgarry land: a one-legged chestnut charger was harnessed to draw it, and right through the horse's body the pole of the car had passed, made fast to a halter across his forehead with a wedge. A red woman sat in the chariot, bright red were her eyebrows, a crimson cloak about her whose folds touched the plain, and close by her side a mighty giant strode, on his back a two-forked hazel staff, goading a cow that shambled on before. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: 'Ye who drive that cow do wrong, for against her will do ye drive her!' cried Cuchulainn. 'Not to thee doth that cow belong.' The woman's name was unpronounceable — Coom-diewr-folt-skayv-garry-skye-ooa; the giant was Darry I mac Feena, and she was driving a cow home in fee for a poem. Cuchulainn leaped at the chariot, set his spear-point on her head, and bade her cease her sharp weapon-play and tell her name; her song was a song of insult, and when he sprang again the woman, the horse, the chariot, the cow and the man disappeared — she passed into the shape of a black bird on a bough. 'As a woman of danger I know you,' he cried. 'Evil in sooth can I send; of thy Bringer of Death I am guardian, shall guard it till cometh thine end. From the Under-world Country of Croghan this cow have I driven... So long as her calf be a yearling, for that time thy life shall endure; but then shall the dread Raid of Cualgne have beginning.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905; not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase: 'Thou shalt see me return alive from the Táin!' vowed Cuchulainn. 'How canst thou that strife be surviving?' sang the woman: when he contends with a hero as fearful and as strong as himself, 'then, in shape of an eel round thee coiling, thy feet at the Ford I will bind'; he swore he would break her on a green stone; then 'as a wolf myself shaping, I will spring on thee eager to slay, I will tear the flesh from thy chest from arm to arm'; he vowed spear-blows would force her to fly; then she would come 'as a heifer, white-skinned, but with ears that are red,' and a hundred white red-eared cows trampling him would take his head from him. The Morrígan, the great Battle Queen, departed with her cow to Rath Croghan and was seen no more by Cuchulainn — and the region took the name of the Clay-land of Evil from her deeds. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Leahy 1905; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: A. H. Leahy, Heroic Romances of Ireland, Vol. II, London 1905 (public domain); underlying: Táin Bó Regamna, ed. and trans. Ernst Windisch, Irische Texte II (1887), public domain

narrative.en:
Before the Táin begins, the war-goddess comes to audit the hero — the Táin Bó Regamna is the auditors' story that prices Cuchulainn's fate in cattle, prophecy and unpronounceable names.

At Dun Imrid lay Cuchulainn and slept, when a cry rang out from the north; he woke and fell with the thud of a weight to the ground. At the ford of the Double Wonder a chariot rattled toward them from the clay-soiled Coolgarry land, and it was harnessed wrongly on purpose: a one-legged chestnut charger drew it, the chariot-pole passing right through the horse's body, made fast to a halter across the forehead with a wedge — a vehicle from nightmare, driven by physics that deny the animal. In it sat a red woman, her eyebrows bright red, her crimson cloak's folds touching the plain, with two poles behind her and her mantle streaming between; and a mighty giant strode by her side with a two-forked hazel staff on his back, goading a shuffling cow ahead.

'Ye who drive that cow do wrong, for against her will do ye drive her!' cried Cuchulainn, claiming the cattle of Ulster as his to guard — and got only insoluble names for answer: the man was Uar-gaeth-sceo-luachair-sceo, then Faebor-begbeoil-cuimdiuir-folt-seenb-gairit-sceo-uath; the woman Coom-diewr-folt-skayv-garry-skye-ooa. Then he admitted the man's name was plain Darry I mac Feena, owner of the Dun of Cúailnge itself, and the cow was the fee for a poem. Cuchulainn sprang at the chariot, set his spear-point on her head and demanded her true name; her song was a song of insult; and when he sprang again, woman, horse, chariot, cow and man vanished together — she into the shape of a black bird on a bough. 'As a woman of danger I know you, and as powerful in spell!' 'Evil in sooth can I send. Of thy Bringer of Death I am guardian, and shall guard it till cometh thine end: from the Under-world Country of Croghan this cow have I driven, to breed by the Dun Bull of Darry mac Feena; so long as her calf be a yearling, for that time thy life shall endure; but then shall the dread Raid of Cúailnge have beginning.'

Then the duel of futures. He vowed to return alive from the Táin with bards singing of it; she sang the terms of his death with the three shapes she would wear against him — an eel coiling round his feet at the ford ('on a green stone by me shall be broken that eel,' he swore), a wolf springing on him to tear the flesh from his chest ('I will force thee to fly with blows of my spear-shaft'), and a white-skinned, red-eared heifer among a hundred red-eared cows, trampling him at a lake by the ford so that his head is smitten from him ('a stone for a cast will I take... thy right or thy left leg will break'). He promised her the wounds; she promised him the shapes; and the great Battle Queen went with her cow to Rath Croghan and was seen no more by Cuchulainn — and the ground took the name of the Clay-land of Evil from her deeds. Every promise in this tale is paid in full in the Táin's ford combats: a prophecy written in the grammar of livestock.
narrative.zh: 《奪牛記》開始之前，戰神即來查帳——雷甘那牛劫記即以牛群、預言與不可讀之名為庫丘林之命定價之查帳故事。庫丘林臥於敦·伊姆里德而眠，北方呼聲驚起；醒時如負重物砰然倒地。於「雙奇渡口」，一輛戰車自泥地庫爾加里嘎然而來，其轅故意錯配：一匹獨腿栗色馬拉之、車轅貫穿馬體、以楔固於額前之籠頭——噩夢之車、否定動物之物理。車中坐一紅衣女子，眉如赤霞、深紅披風之褶觸地；身側一偉岸巨人，背負兩叉榛杖，驅一頭蹣跚之牛於前。『驅牛者行不義，此牛非自願而行！』庫丘林喊道，稱阿爾斯特牛群盡屬他護——得到的只是不可解之名：其人先名烏爾-蓋特-斯凱歐-盧阿希爾-斯凱歐，又名法博爾-貝格貝奧爾-庫姆迪維爾-福爾特-塞恩布-加里特-斯凱歐-烏阿特；其女名庫姆-迪埃爾-福爾特-斯凱夫-加里-斯凱歐-烏阿。然後他承認其人名為達里·麥克·菲納——庫利環堡之主本身——而牛乃一首詩之酬金。庫丘林撲向戰車、矛尖置其首、索其真名；她的歌是一首侮辱之詩；他再度撲去時，女子、馬、戰車、牛與人一同消失——她化為枝上一黑鳥。『我識得你，危險之女，咒術強大！』『我能降禍於你。我是你死亡使者之守護者，必守至你終結之時：我自克魯亨冥世之地驅牛而來、與達里之棕牛相伴；其犢未滿歲，你命尚存；犢一歲，可怖的庫利牛劫便將開始。』繼而是未來之決鬥。他誓將自奪牛記生還、得吟遊詩人之歌；她則唱出他死亡之條款與她將化之三形——渡口纏繞其足之鰻（他誓將她於綠石上擊碎）、撕裂其胸膛之狼（他誓以矛桿之擊迫使她逃）、與百頭紅耳牛群中踐踏他的白身紅耳牝牛（他誓以彈石斷其右腿或左腿）。他許以傷，她許以形；偉大的戰后攜牛往拉思克羅根而去，庫丘林再未見她——該地因她之事而得「惡土」之名。此篇中每句諾言皆於《奪牛記》渡口之戰中全數兌現：以牲畜之文法寫成之預言。

functions: Prophecy of the hero's death in cattle grammar: fate priced as livestock and calf-years

The unpronounceable-name riddling: power withheld through names that cannot be spoken
Etiology of the Clay-land of Evil (Grellach Dolluid) and of the cow that breeds the Táin's bull-war
